newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees new trade pact with U.S., Canada.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees new trade pact with U.S., Canada.

text.p: The European Union, Canada and United States have agreed to recognise each others certification and standards procedures on products worth over $40 billion a year in transatlantic trade.

The European Commission said on Friday that the Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA) will cover bilateral trade in products ranging from telecoms and electronic equipment to pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

Through the agreement, Washington will allow European companies to sell products in the United States immediately after they have been tested and certified to U.S. health, safety and quality standards in Europe, forgoing the need to carry out a second set of tests in America.
The same applies vice-versa as well as to trade between the EU and Canada.

"It is no exaggeration to say this is the single most important economic development between the United States and European Union for the past few years," said Peter Guilford, spokesman for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

"It covers growth industries ... it will help lead to greater conformity in global standards and will greatly slash through the red tape that sometimes confronts exporters and importers on both sides of the Atlantic," he said.
Brittan said in a statement that the MRA was "the crowning achievement of the new transatlantic relationship".

The pact -- already initialled by Canada but due to be signed by Washington next week -- comes after three years of governmental wrangling over the issue and close cooperation between industries on both sides of the Atlantic.

The Transatlantic Business Dialogue (TABD), a group of industrial and business experts from the EU and U.S. did much of the ground work in harmonising certification procedures to smooth the way for an agreement.
The Information Technology Council estimates the deal will save the U.S. and European IT industry some $1.37 billion a year.

The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries Associations said the agreement would help get rid of "the current need to perform duplicate inspections ... a direct and unnecessary cost for governments, regulatory authorities and manufacturers ... at the expense of patients themselves".

The main sectors covered by the agreement are medicinal products, medical devices, telecoms terminal equipment, electromagnetic computability, electrical safety and recreational craft such as speed boats and sailing yachts.
Other sectors -- notably veterinary vaccines -- will be added to the agreement in the future.

Although certification experts were swift to point out that many products would still require testing to two or three sets of standards, in many cases this could be done at the same time and now also at one place.

"In the past, if you were testing a blue ball-point pen to check it was blue, the test had to be repeated in the United States," one European Commission official said. "Now, even if the U.S. says all blue ball-points need to have a pocket clip, that can be tested and certified here."
Exporters say this can save considerable time and money -- particularly for products at the cutting edge of technology where they may have a limited shelf-life or consumer value.
Swedish electronic giant Ericsson, for example, has said the life-cyle of a mobile phone model was just 18 months and it currently took three months to get certification in the U.S.
"An MRA will therefore bring an appreciable reduction in 'time-to-market' and thus improved commercial conditions," the company said.
